title: The Daily Decree
blurb: One location riddle a day, the same for everyone, new at midnight San Francisco time. Solve it and share your result.

pool.riddle: Locals call me Big Pointy. I was the tallest building in the city from 1972 until 2017, and I stand on the old shoreline of Yerba Buena Cove.
hints: The Financial District, on Montgomery Street.
pool.fact: A grove of redwoods transplanted from the Santa Cruz Mountains grows in Redwood Park at its base.

pool.riddle: I was built in 1933 with a socialite's bequest and painted inside by more than twenty muralists, on the hill that once signaled the ships.
pool.fact: Coit Tower is 210 feet of unpainted reinforced concrete, designed by Arthur Brown Jr. and Henry Temple Howard.

pool.riddle: I was designed in 1915 to look like a Roman ruin, and I was so loved that they rebuilt me rather than let me become one.
pool.fact: It is the only structure from the 1915 Panama-Pacific Exposition still on its original site. Its rotunda is 162 feet high.

pool.riddle: My clock tower rises 245 feet at the foot of Market Street, and each of my four clock faces is 22 feet across. Boats still dock behind me.
hints: The Embarcadero, at the foot of Market Street.
pool.fact: Designed by A. Page Brown and completed in 1898, it came through both the 1906 and 1989 earthquakes with little damage.

pool.riddle: My color was chosen to stand out in the fog. The Navy wanted me striped black and yellow. Fly to the middle of my main span.
hints: The strait between San Francisco and Marin.
pool.fact: Opened May 27, 1937, its main span is 4,200 feet and its towers rise 746 feet above the water.

pool.riddle: Lighthouse, fortress, federal prison, and for 19 months a homeland reclaimed. Nearly 1.4 million people visit me each year.
hints: An island in the bay, north of Fisherman's Wharf.
pool.fact: The first lighthouse on the US West Coast was lit here in 1854; today's tower replaced it in 1909. The penitentiary closed on March 21, 1963.

pool.riddle: We are a pair, about 925 feet tall near the center of the city, and still we are only the second and third highest. Fly to us.
hints: Near the geographic center of San Francisco.
pool.fact: Only Mount Davidson, at 928 feet, rises higher than Twin Peaks inside the city.

pool.riddle: A white palace of glass and wood, finished in 1879, the oldest building in the city's biggest park.
hints: The eastern end of Golden Gate Park.
pool.fact: It is the oldest remaining municipal wooden conservatory in the United States.

pool.riddle: A fine arts museum named for an early newspaperman, on the Music Concourse in the park. Almost a million visitors came through my doors in 2023.
hints: The Music Concourse in Golden Gate Park.
pool.fact: The de Young had 999,645 visitors in 2023 and shares its management with the Legion of Honor.

pool.riddle: My dome is 42 feet taller than the one in Washington. I reopened in 1915 after my predecessor fell in 1906.
pool.fact: Architect Arthur Brown Jr. cared about every detail of City Hall, down to the doorknobs and the typeface.

pool.riddle: My adobe chapel was finished in 1791. I am the oldest intact building in the city.
hints: The Mission District, at 16th and Dolores streets.
pool.fact: The mission was founded in 1776, and Ohlone people provided most of the labor that built its chapel.

pool.riddle: Brick and granite beneath an arch of steel, guarding the narrowest part of the Golden Gate since before the Civil War.
hints: Directly under the south end of the Golden Gate Bridge.
pool.fact: Builders blasted a 90-foot cliff down to 15 feet above the water so cannonballs could skip into enemy ships.

pool.riddle: In 1896 I was the largest indoor swimming establishment in the world. Since 1966 I am concrete ruins that the ocean fills for free.
hints: Lands End, just north of the Cliff House.
pool.fact: The Sutro Baths opened on March 14, 1896, and burned to the foundations in June 1966.

pool.riddle: Shops, a two-story carousel and a colony of sea lions who moved in uninvited in 1989.
pool.fact: California sea lions first hauled out on Pier 39 in September 1989, a few weeks before the Loma Prieta earthquake.

pool.riddle: More than 300 mechanical arcade machines, one of the largest privately owned collections in the world. Bring coins.
pool.fact: Its founder, Ed Zelinsky, began collecting at age 11.

pool.riddle: Once a woolen mill and a chocolate company, now a square of shops at the foot of Russian Hill.
pool.fact: Part of the square is listed on the National Register of Historic Places as Pioneer Woolen Mills and D. Ghirardelli Company.

pool.riddle: A free museum inside a working powerhouse. Look down and you can watch the wheels that pull the cables under the streets.
hints: Nob Hill, at Washington and Mason.
pool.fact: Grip car No. 8 from the 1873 Clay Street Hill Railroad is preserved here.

pool.riddle: Copies of Florence's Gates of Paradise, two labyrinths and a carillon of forty-four bells, high on Nob Hill.
pool.fact: Grace Cathedral's parish was founded in 1849 and lost its earlier church in the 1906 earthquake.

pool.riddle: Established in 1847, I am one of the city's first parks, with an Italian church on my edge and cafes all around.
pool.fact: Washington Square is a 2.8-acre park in North Beach, across from Saints Peter and Paul Church.

pool.riddle: The first all-paperback bookstore in the country, and the publisher of a poem that went on trial.
pool.fact: In 1957 Judge Clayton Horn ruled that Allen Ginsberg's Howl was not obscene, a landmark free speech decision.

pool.riddle: The Italian Cathedral of the West, with Masses in English, Italian and Cantonese, facing Washington Square.
pool.fact: The church is administered by the Salesians of Don Bosco and is the home church of the city's Italian-American community.

pool.riddle: A gift from the Republic of China in 1969, I mark the southern entrance of the oldest Chinatown in North America.
pool.fact: The Dragon Gate is one of the most photographed places in Chinatown.

pool.riddle: The city's first park, where the American flag went up in 1846 and gold was announced in 1848.
pool.fact: Portsmouth Square was named for the USS Portsmouth, whose men raised the flag here.

pool.riddle: An actress's gift to the city in 1875 that became the meeting place after the 1906 earthquake.
hints: Market Street, where Geary and Kearny meet it.
pool.fact: Lotta Crabtree commissioned it. Survivors of 1906 gathered here at 5:12 a.m. every April 18.

pool.riddle: My first version burned in 1906. I reopened on the same corner of Market and New Montgomery in 1909.
pool.fact: The new Palace Hotel opened on December 19, 1909, and was renovated and seismically retrofitted from 1989 to 1991.

pool.riddle: The first museum on the West Coast devoted solely to 20th-century art, with more than 33,000 works.
hints: Third Street in SoMa, beside Yerba Buena Gardens.
The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art.
pool.fact: SFMOMA displays its collection in 170,000 square feet of exhibition space.

pool.riddle: Nicknamed the Granite Lady, I pressed the nation's coins from 1874 to 1937 and survived 1906.
pool.fact: The Old Mint was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1961.

pool.riddle: A museum of Asian art whose building and collection belong to the city, in the Civic Center.
pool.fact: Its full name is the Asian Art Museum of San Francisco, Chong-Moon Lee Center for Asian Art and Culture.

pool.riddle: Home of the San Francisco Opera since 1932, and the room where the United Nations first assembled in 1945.
hints: Van Ness Avenue, behind City Hall.
pool.fact: The Treaty of San Francisco, restoring peace between Japan and the Allies, was signed here in September 1951.

pool.riddle: Short, golden and heroic. In 1906 I kept the water flowing and saved a neighborhood from the fire.
hints: A corner of Dolores Park, at 20th and Church.
pool.fact: It is painted gold every April 18, except in 2012, when someone bought silver by mistake.

pool.riddle: Bounded by 18th and 20th, Dolores and Church, I am the city's favorite sunny lawn, two blocks south of a mission.
hints: The western edge of the Mission District.
pool.fact: The northern end of Dolores Park faces Mission High School.

pool.riddle: A plaza where Market, Castro and 17th streets meet, above the stairs to the Muni Metro, named for a beloved city supervisor.
hints: The Castro, where Market Street meets Castro Street.
pool.fact: Harvey Milk Plaza serves as the southern entrance to Castro station.

pool.riddle: Two streets crossed and gave their names to a counterculture. Find the corner.
hints: The corner of Haight and Ashbury.
pool.fact: The Haight-Ashbury became the center of the 1967 Summer of Love.

pool.riddle: Established in 1867 as Hill Park, I am the oldest official park in the city, rising 575 feet above Haight Street.
hints: Between Haight Street and Buena Vista Avenue.
pool.fact: Buena Vista Park covers 38.3 acres on a steep hill.

pool.riddle: A hill that is also an island, in a lake that is in a park, in a city on a peninsula.
hints: The middle of Golden Gate Park.
pool.fact: Strawberry Hill occupies an entire island in Blue Heron Lake, connected to the park by two bridges.

pool.riddle: The younger of the two windmills at the western edge of Golden Gate Park, completed in 1908 on the south side.
hints: The western edge of Golden Gate Park, near Ocean Beach.
pool.fact: The Murphy Windmill was added to the San Francisco Designated Landmark list in 2000.

pool.riddle: A Spanish Colonial Revival building at the very western end of Golden Gate Park, facing the ocean.
hints: The Great Highway, at the end of Golden Gate Park.
pool.fact: The Beach Chalet has been a San Francisco Designated Landmark since 1985.

pool.riddle: A giant camera you can stand inside, perched beside the Cliff House on the headland.
hints: Lands End, next to the Cliff House.
pool.fact: The Camera Obscura was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2001.

pool.riddle: A memorial on the cliffs at Lands End to a cruiser that earned 17 battle stars.
hints: The Coastal Trail at Lands End.
pool.fact: USS San Francisco was one of the most decorated U.S. ships of World War II.

pool.riddle: Half a mile of sand just south of the Golden Gate, with the bridge as the backdrop for every photo.
hints: The Pacific shore of the Presidio.
pool.fact: Battery Chamberlin, a seacoast artillery battery built in 1904, sits at Baker Beach.

pool.riddle: Twenty-five pipes and no keyboard. The bay plays me, best at high tide.
hints: The tip of the jetty by the yacht club in the Marina.
pool.fact: Its stones were salvaged from the demolished Laurel Hill Cemetery.

pool.riddle: A former Army airfield on a filled-in marsh, now a shoreline park with the marsh brought back.
hints: The northern shore of the Presidio, east of the Golden Gate Bridge.
pool.fact: Crissy Field closed as an airfield after 1974 and the National Park Service took control in 1994.

pool.riddle: During World War II I was the principal port for the Pacific campaign. Now my piers hold theaters and galleries.
hints: Between the Marina and Aquatic Park.
pool.fact: Fort Mason was named in 1882 for Richard Barnes Mason, a military governor before statehood.

pool.riddle: A museum about a famous animator's life, facing the Presidio's parade ground, opened in 2009.
pool.fact: The museum opened on October 1, 2009, at 104 Montgomery Street in the Presidio.

pool.riddle: A 70-foot bow and arrow planted beside the Embarcadero, as if a giant had missed.
hints: Rincon Park, south of the Ferry Building.
pool.fact: Claes Oldenburg and Coosje van Bruggen made it, commissioned by Gap founders Donald and Doris Fisher.

pool.riddle: A small oval park in SoMa, wrapped by its own looping street, between Second and Third.
pool.fact: South Park covers just 0.85 acres.

pool.riddle: A drawbridge that lifts to let boats through, carrying Third Street over Mission Creek beside the ballpark.
pool.fact: The bascule bridge was originally called the Third Street Bridge.

pool.riddle: A campus at the foot of Telegraph Hill that holds the headquarters of a famous blue jeans company.
hints: The eastern foot of Telegraph Hill.
pool.fact: A business reporter once called it the only true corporate campus in San Francisco.

pool.riddle: A temple to the sea goddess Mazu, founded around 1852, on a Chinatown street that takes its Chinese name from me.
pool.fact: It is one of the oldest Chinese temples still operating in the United States.

pool.riddle: Rocks just off the Cliff House where sea lions haul out, though my name gives the credit to seals.
hints: Just offshore from the Cliff House.
pool.fact: Both Steller and California sea lions haul out on Seal Rocks.

pool.riddle: A bandshell from 1900, a gift from a sugar magnate, and one of the largest in North America.
hints: The Music Concourse in Golden Gate Park.
pool.fact: Claus Spreckels gave the bandshell to the city.

pool.riddle: A wooded lane on Russian Hill with wooden steps and bay views. A novelist turned me into Barbary Lane.
hints: Russian Hill, between Leavenworth and Taylor.
pool.fact: Armistead Maupin confirmed Macondray Lane inspired Barbary Lane in Tales of the City.

pool.riddle: One block, eight hairpin turns, and up to 17,000 visitors on a busy summer day.
hints: The crooked block of Lombard Street.
pool.fact: Surveyor Jasper O'Farrell named it after Lombard Street in Philadelphia.

pool.riddle: At 928 feet I am the highest natural point in San Francisco, with a 103-foot cross on my crown.
hints: South of Twin Peaks, past Portola Drive.
pool.fact: Each Easter a prayer service is held here and the cross is illuminated.

pool.riddle: A one-block alley where nearly every garage door and fence has been a mural since 1973.
pool.fact: Balmy Alley is in the Calle 24 Latino Cultural District.

pool.riddle: The city's largest convention center, opened in 1981 and named for a mayor.
hints: South of Market, along Howard Street.
pool.fact: The Moscone Center spreads three main halls across three blocks.

pool.riddle: A sloping lawn between the Conservatory of Flowers and Haight Street where drum circles start on their own.
hints: The eastern end of Golden Gate Park.
pool.fact: Hippie Hill looks out over Robin Williams Meadow.

pool.riddle: At 1,070 feet I am the tallest building in San Francisco, and in 2018 I took that title from a three-legged tower.
hints: Mission Street, between First and Fremont.
pool.fact: Designed by Cesar Pelli, it was the last of his buildings completed in his lifetime.

pool.riddle: Four office towers, two hotels and an ice rink every winter, between Clay and Sacramento streets.
hints: The Financial District, just west of the Ferry Building.
pool.fact: Offices at Embarcadero Center hold about 14,000 people.

pool.riddle: Hidden under a lawn in the Sunset, I am the city's largest reservoir, with 720 columns holding up my roof.
pool.fact: The underground reservoir was completed in 1960.

pool.riddle: A 12.9-acre park capping the western edge of Pacific Heights, named for a spring.
hints: Pacific Heights, west of Lafayette Park.
pool.fact: Alta Plaza Park takes its name from an eponymous spring.

pool.riddle: Eight blocks long and one block wide, I am the handle of the city's biggest park.
pool.fact: The Panhandle is three-quarters of a mile long and is cut in half by Masonic Avenue.

pool.riddle: A dell in eastern Golden Gate Park, set aside as a national place to remember those lost to AIDS.
hints: The de Laveaga Dell in Golden Gate Park.
pool.fact: The Grove is a national memorial where people touched by HIV and AIDS gather to heal and remember.

pool.riddle: Fifty-five acres holding nearly 9,000 kinds of plants, once known as Strybing Arboretum.
hints: Golden Gate Park, near Ninth Avenue.
pool.fact: It is one of the three Gardens of Golden Gate Park, with the Japanese Tea Garden and the Conservatory of Flowers.

pool.riddle: Three and a half miles of sand, strong currents and famous fog along the city's western edge.
hints: The Pacific side of the city.
pool.fact: Ocean Beach is part of the Golden Gate National Recreation Area.

pool.riddle: A park above the Cliff House on a mayor's old estate, looking down on Seal Rocks.
hints: Above the Cliff House at Lands End.
pool.fact: Sutro Heights Park is part of the Sutro Historic District.

pool.riddle: One of only four cemeteries inside the city limits, resting in the Presidio.
hints: The Presidio, near the Main Post.
pool.fact: San Francisco banned new burials in 1900 and later moved most of its graves to Colma, which is why so few cemeteries remain.
